title: Plasma Polyamines and Short‐Term Adverse Outcomes Among Patients With Ischemic Stroke: A Prospective Cohort Study
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.abstract:
Polyamines have been reported to be associated with neurological function, but the associations between polyamines and the prognosis of ischemic stroke remain unclear. We aimed to prospectively investigate whether elevated plasma polyamine levels are associated with adverse outcomes in patients with ischemic stroke.

Plasma polyamine levels were measured at admission in 3570 patients with acute ischemic stroke, and clinical outcomes were assessed at 3 months after stroke onset. The primary outcome was a composite outcome of death and major disability (modified Rankin Scale score≥3), and secondary outcomes included the individual outcomes of death and major disability. During a 3‐month follow‐up period, 877 participants (25.1%) experienced the primary outcome. Increased putrescines were associated with a decreased risk of the primary outcome (the highest versus the lowest tertile: odds ratio, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.58–0.91]; P =0.005) and major disability (odds ratio, 0.59 [95% CI, 0.47–0.74]; P <0.001). Conversely, increased spermidines were associated with an increased risk of death (hazard ratio, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.10–3.14]; P =0.020), and increased spermines were associated with an increased risk of the primary outcome (odds ratio, 1.36 [95% CI, 1.08–1.71]; P =0.009) and major disability (odds ratio, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.01–1.59]; P =0.041).

Among patients with ischemic stroke, high plasma putrescine levels were associated with a decreased risk of adverse outcomes, whereas high plasma spermidine and spermine levels were associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes. Further studies are needed to investigate whether targeting these polyamines can improve the prognosis of patients with ischemic stroke.

sections.methods:
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

The present study was conducted on the basis of the participants and data from CATIS, a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted from August 2009 to May 2013. Details on the CATIS trial protocol, statistical analysis plan, and main results have been published previously. 12 In summary, CATIS recruited 4071 consecutive patients aged ≥22 years in 26 hospitals across China within 48 hours of stroke onset with high systolic blood pressure (BP) (140 to <220 mm Hg). Patients with a BP ≥220/120 mm Hg, cerebrovascular stenosis (≥70%), acute myocardial infarction, severe heart failure, unstable angina, atrial fibrillation, aortic dissection, resistant hypertension, and those in deep coma as well as patients treated with intravenous thrombolytic therapy were excluded from CATIS. In this study, 501 participants were further excluded because their plasma samples were not available or some collected samples were hemolyzed during the collection or separation process. In total, 3570 participants were included in this study (Figure S1 ). Written consent was obtained from all study participants or their immediate relatives before data collection. CATIS was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov ( NCT01840072 ) and approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Soochow University in China and Tulane University in the United States.

At baseline, trained nurses and physicians conducted face‐to‐face surveys to collect information on demographic characteristics and medical history (eg, family history of stroke and coronary heart disease). All physical examinations were performed according to the standardized protocols. Stroke severity was assessed by trained neurologists at admission using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). 13 Ischemic stroke subtype was classified as large‐artery atherosclerosis (thrombotic), cardiac embolism (embolic), and small‐artery occlusion lacunae (lacunar) on the basis of TOAST (Trial of ORG 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment) criteria according to the protocol of CATIS. 14 Three BP measurements were taken by trained nurses at recruitment using a standard mercury sphygmomanometer and following the protocol recommended by the American Heart Association, and the mean of the 3 measurements was used for the analyses. 15 The estimated glomerular filtration rate was calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration cystatin C equation. 16 According to Chinese guidelines on the prevention and treatment of dyslipidemia, dyslipidemia was defined as total cholesterol ≥6.22 mmol/L, triglyceride ≥2.26 mmol/L, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥4.14 mmol/L, high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol <1.04 mmol/L, or self‐reported history of physician‐diagnosed dyslipidemia. 17

Blood samples were drawn with EDTA tubes for all the participants within 24 hours of hospital admission after at least an 8‐hour fast. Plasma samples were separated at the clinical laboratories of the participating hospitals and immediately stored at −80°C until testing. Plasma polyamines were quantified on ultra‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (ACQUITY UPLC I‐Class/Xevo TQ‐S; Waters Corp., Milford, MA), using commercial putrescine (51799; 100 mg, Sigma‐Aldrich, Burlington, MA), spermidine (49761; 100 mg; Sigma‐Aldrich), and spermine (ZC‐52886; 100 mg; Shanghai Zzbio Co., Ltd., Shaghai, China) as internal standards. The metabolites were chromatographically eluted with 0.1% formic acid water and 0.1% formic acid acetonitrile after 5‐μL aliquots of metabolite extract injected, and separated on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm, Waters Corp.) at 45°C. The chromatographic gradient ramped from 50% (weak elution) to 99% in 5 minutes, setting a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min. In multiple rection monitoring mode (electrospray ionization in positive mode), the main parameters of the mass spectrometer were optimized to desolvation gas flow 1000 L/h, source temperature 150°C, desolvation temperature 500°C, and capillary voltage 3 kv. Quality control and blank samples were interspersed in the whole detection procession. The raw data files were processed using MassLynx software version 4.1 (Waters Corp.) to perform peak integration, calibration, and quantitation for each metabolite. Laboratory technicians who measured the plasma polyamines were blinded to the clinical features and outcomes of the study participants.

The participants were followed up in person at 3 months after acute ischemic stroke by trained neurologists unaware of the baseline characteristics and concentration of plasma polyamines. The primary outcome was a combination of death and major disability (modified Rankin Scale score≥3) in this study. Secondary outcomes included individual outcomes of death and major disability. The modified Rankin Scale scores ranged from 0 to 6, with 0 indicating no symptoms, 5 indicating severe disability (ie, bedridden, incontinent, or requiring constant nursing care and attention), and 6 indicating death. Death certificates were obtained for the deceased patients, and hospital data were abstracted for vascular events. The study outcome assessment committee, blinded to the treatment assignment, reviewed and adjudicated subsequent outcomes following the criteria established in the Antihypertensive and Lipid‐Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial.

Baseline data of the participants were compared according to the primary outcome status at 3 months after stroke and were presented as number (percentage), median (interquartile range), or mean (SD). Differences in baseline characteristics were analyzed using the χ 2 test for categorical variables and variance analysis for continuous variables. We also compared the baseline characteristics according to the tertiles of plasma putrescine, spermidine, and spermine concentrations. Testing for the linear trend of baseline characteristics across the tertiles of these 3 polyamines was performed with generalized linear regression analysis for continuous variables and the Cochran–Armitage trend χ 2 test for categorical variables. Associations between plasma polyamines and both primary outcome and major disability were assessed using multivariable logistic regression models. In these analyses, primary outcome and major disability were modeled as binary dependent variables, while plasma polyamine levels were categorized into tertiles as independent variables. We adjusted for important prognostic covariates, including age, sex, current smoking, alcohol drinking, admission systolic BP, dyslipidemia, baseline NIHSS score, estimated glomerular filtration rate, time from stroke onset to hospitalization, medical history of coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke subtype, and antihypertensive treatment after admission to hospital. Adjusted odds ratios and 95% CIs were calculated for higher tertiles compared with the lowest tertile. We checked the proportional hazards assumption using Schoenfeld residuals (all global test P >0.05) and functional forms of covariates using Martingale residuals. Associations with death were examined using Cox proportional hazards regression models, with the same set of covariates as the logistic regression models. In these analyses, we modeled death as the dependent variable, and the plasma polyamine levels as independent variables categorized into tertiles. Adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and their 95% CIs) were calculated for higher tertiles compared with the lowest tertile. In addition, we tested for an ordinal association between plasma polyamine tertiles and the primary outcome and major disability using logistic regression models and assessed the association between polyamine tertiles and time to death using Cox proportional hazards regression models, treating the plasma polyamine tertiles as an ordinal variable. Furthermore, restricted cubic splines were used to examine the shape of the association between plasma polyamines and primary outcome with 4 knots (at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles). 18

Subgroup analyses were further conducted to evaluate whether age, sex, current cigarette smoking status, current alcohol consumption status, and other important factors would modify the significant associations identified through multivariable logistic regression analyses. Interactions between the significant plasma polyamines and subgroup variables on primary outcome were tested in the models with interaction terms by likelihood ratio test, adjusting for the covariates mentioned above. Sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the study results by using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for multiple imputations of missing covariates to address possible biases caused by missing data. In addition, multivariable ordinal logistic regression models were performed to evaluate the associations between the plasma polyamines and modified Rankin Scale shift with adjustment for the aforementioned variables. Significance was defined as a 2‐tailed P value of 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS statistical software version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).
sections.results:
A total of 3570 participants (2275 men and 1295 women) with a mean age of 61.8 years were included in the present study. Most baseline characteristics were balanced between participants assayed for plasma polyamines and those not assayed (Table S1 ), indicating that the participants assayed for plasma polyamines represent the total participants of CATIS. Compared with the participants without the primary outcome, those with the primary outcome tended to be older and female; had a higher prevalence of history of coronary heart disease, thrombotic and embolic stroke subtype, higher systolic BP, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, baseline NIHSS score, spermidine, and spermine; had a lower prevalence of cigarette smoking, alcohol drinking, and lacunar stroke subtype; had lower triglyceride and estimated glomerular filtration rate levels; and had a shorter time from onset to hospitalization (Table 1 ). Additional details on baseline characteristics according to the tertiles of plasma polyamines are shown in Tables S2 through S4 .

Baseline Population Characteristics According to Primary Outcome Status at 3 Months in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

BP indicates blood pressure; mRS, modified Rankin Scale; and NIHSS, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale.

Continuous variables are expressed as mean±SD or as median (interquartile range) and are compared by Student's t tests or Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests. Categorical variables are expressed as frequency (%) and are compared by χ 2 tests.

Within 3 months after ischemic stroke, 75 participants (2.1%) were lost to follow‐up. Among the remaining participants, 877 participants (25.1%) experienced the primary outcome. After adjusting for age, sex, baseline NIHSS score, and other important covariates, higher plasma putrescine levels were significantly associated with lower risks of adverse outcomes, whereas higher plasma spermidine or spermine levels were significantly associated with higher risks of adverse outcomes (Table 2 ). Specifically, the adjusted odds ratios for tertile 3 versus 1 of plasma putrescine were 0.72 (95% CI, 0.58–0.91; P =0.005) for the primary outcome ( P for trend=0.005), and 0.59 (95% CI, 0.47–0.74; P <0.001) for major disability ( P for trend <0.001). Conversely, the adjusted HR for tertile 3 versus 1 of plasma spermidine was 1.86 (95% CI, 1.10–3.14; P =0.020) for death ( P for trend=0.016). The adjusted odds ratios for tertile 3 versus 1 of plasma spermine were 1.36 (95% CI, 1.08–1.71; P =0.009) for the primary outcome ( P for trend=0.01), and 1.27 (95% CI, 1.01–1.59; P =0.041) for major disability ( P for trend=0.048; Table 2 ). Sensitivity analyses further confirmed these findings (Table S5 ). Multivariable ordinal logistic regression analyses showed a significantly better shift in the distribution of the modified Rankin Scale score, with higher putrescine tertiles in patients with ischemic stroke ( P for trend=0.008; Table S6 ). When looking at the shape of associations between continuous polyamines and the primary outcome, there was a dose–response relationship between plasma putrescine concentrations and the primary outcome at 3 months after ischemic stroke ( P for linearity=0.006) ( Figure ). Additionally, spermine showed a nonlinear association with the primary outcome at 3 months after ischemic stroke ( P for nonlinearity=0.024).

Model 2 was further adjusted for ischemic stroke subtype and antihypertensive treatment after admission to hospital on the basis of model 1.

Odds ratios and 95% CIs derived from restricted cubic spline regression, with knots placed at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles of the distribution of plasma polyamines. The reference point for polyamines is the midpoint (3.93 ng/mL for putrescine, 3.85 ng/mL for spermidine, and 2.85 ng/mL for spermine) of the reference group from categorical analysis. Odds ratios were adjusted for age, sex, current smoking, alcohol drinking, admission systolic blood pressure, dyslipidemia, baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score, estimated glomerular filtration rate, time from stroke onset to hospitalization, ischemic stroke subtype, medical history of coronary heart disease, and antihypertensive treatment after admission to hospital.

In the subgroup analyses stratified by age, sex, current cigarette smoking, current alcohol consumption, baseline systolic BP, history of coronary heart disease, and receiving immediate BP reduction, the results consistently showed that patients with higher levels of putrescine were more likely to have a reduced risk of the primary outcome compared with patients with lower plasma putrescine levels. In contrast, those with higher spermine levels were more likely to have an increased risk of the primary outcome when compared with patients with the lowest plasma spermine level across all subgroups (Table 3 ). No interaction was observed between plasma putrescine and spermine and subgroup factors on the risk of the primary outcome (all P values for interaction >0.05).

Subgroup Analysis of Adjusted Odds Ratios (95% CIs) of Primary Outcome at 3 Months After Ischemic Stroke With Putrescine and Spermine Tertiles at Baseline

In the multivariable models, confounding factors such as age, sex, current smoking, alcohol drinking, admission systolic blood pressure, dyslipidemia, baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score, estimated glomerular filtration rate, time from stroke onset to hospitalization, ischemic stroke subtype, medical history of coronary heart disease, and antihypertensive treatment after admission to hospital were included unless the variable was used as a subgroup variable.
sections.discussion:
The current study was a large‐scale prospective study assessing the associations between polyamines and the prognosis of ischemic stroke. Data on baseline characteristics and study outcomes were collected by trained staff using standardized protocols and rigorous quality control procedures. Our findings revealed that high baseline plasma putrescine levels were associated with a decreased risk of the primary outcome and major disability at 3 months after ischemic stroke, while high spermidine and spermine levels were associated with increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes after adjustment for major confounders. Subgroup analyses further confirmed these findings. The results indicate that plasma putrescine, spermidine, and spermine might be implicated in the pathological progression of ischemic stroke, but further validation through additional studies is necessary.

Putrescine plays a central role in the activator of the polyamine biosynthetic pathway. 7 , 8 Previous animal evidence suggested that putrescine levels were increased in the acute response to ischemia and postischemic recirculation. 8 Lukkarinen et al 9 also reported that putrescine levels were increased in the infarcted and contralateral hemispheres after permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion. Recently, clinical research based on 238 patients with ischemic stroke identified putrescine as a protective indicator for large artery atherosclerosis stroke through the screening of 55 serum metabolites. 19 However, most of these studies were conducted on the basis of laboratory animals with artificial models of cerebral infarction or small sample cases, and no large population‐based studies for stroke prognosis are currently available. In our multicenter study with a large sample size and sufficient statistical power, we found that elevated putrescine levels were associated with a reduced risk of adverse outcomes among patients with ischemic stroke, and there was a dose–response relationship between them after adjustment for potential confounders. Important and comprehensive information about potential confounders including baseline NIHSS score, estimated glomerular filtration rate, time from stroke onset to hospitalization, and ischemic stroke subtype was collected and controlled in the multivariable models. Thus, the methodology of this study is appropriate and rigorous, and our study will provide a valid assessment of the relationship between plasma putrescine and poor prognosis in patients with ischemic stroke.

Spermidine is an abundant natural polyamine synthesized from putrescine. A previous nested case–control study with 101 patients with stroke and 101 matched stroke‐free controls reported that elevated serum spermidine was significantly associated with increased risk of stroke. 10 In addition, Els et al found a significant increase of spermidine levels in patients with focal cerebral ischemia compared with healthy control subjects, and spermidine levels at admission in peripheral red blood cells were positively associated with the infarct volume on days 4 to 6 and with the clinical NIHSS score on day 28. 20 In the present prospective study, patients with elevated baseline spermidine had an increased likelihood of death at 3 months after ischemic stroke. Future studies are warranted to further verify this association.

Spermine is an important endogenous polyamine derived from spermidine, which has been involved in inflammatory conditions and neurogenerative diseases. 21 , 22 In animal models of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion, Duan et al 11 found that exogenous administration of spermine dramatically increased infarct volume and inhibition of spermine synthesis significantly attenuated neuronal damages. This evidence suggested that spermine may be implicated in the progression of ischemic stroke and inhibition of spermine may alleviate ischemic brain damage. To date, there have been no reports on the relationship between spermine and the prognosis among patients with ischemic stroke. In this prospective study, our findings provided evidence supporting the deleterious effect of spermine on the prognosis of acute ischemic stroke; higher spermine levels remain independently associated with increased risk of poor outcomes at 3 months after ischemic stroke when baseline NIHSS score and other potent prognostic factors were included into the multifactorial models. Therefore, our study findings will provide essential population‐based evidence for the detrimental role of spermine in the development of ischemic stroke.

Our study has several clinical implications. We used data from the CATIS, which helps in understanding the pathophysiology of ischemic stroke and identifying the patients with ischemic stroke at high risk who may benefit from enhanced monitoring and targeted therapeutic interventions. We found that patients with high plasma putrescine levels may have a decreased risk of adverse outcomes, whereas those with high plasma spermidine and spermine levels may be at an increased risk of adverse outcomes. These findings suggested that inhibiting spermidine and spermine might decrease the risk of adverse outcomes, and supplementation with putrescine might help improve the prognosis of ischemic stroke. Interestingly, spermine depletion with spermine synthase inhibitors has been explored as a potential therapeutic approach for various types of cancer. 23 Given that the pathobiology of ischemic stroke shares many features with tumorigenesis, 24 , 25 further studies are needed to investigate the clinical benefits of spermidine/spermine synthase inhibitors for ischemic stroke. Further clinical trials are also needed to verify whether increasing putrescine levels improve clinical outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke.

Mechanisms underlying the observed associations between plasma polyamines and clinical poor outcomes after ischemic stroke remain unclear. Putrescine increases after acute ischemic stroke may be an adaptive negative feedback response that limits the adverse effects and promotes recovery by facilitating inflammation to subside and promoting clearance of dead neurons. 26 , 27 Spermidine and spermine are induced to be oxidized through the activation of spermidine/spermine‐N1‐acetyltransferase via the nuclear factor κ‐light‐chain enhancer of activated B cells pathway, resulting in the production of toxic hydrogen peroxide and aldehydes. 28 , 29 , 30 This may exacerbate neuronal cell damage after cerebral infarction. In addition, spermine has been established to exacerbate ischemic neuron injury through neuronal depolarization, cytoplasmic Ca 2+ overload, and sensitizing acid‐sensing ion channels to extracellular acidosis. 11 , 31 Furthermore, an experimental study has observed significant cortical cell death after spermine administration in a rat model of permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion but not after putrescine administration. 29

Our study had some limitations. First, it was based on the CATIS cohort, which excluded patients who had a BP of ≥220/120 mm Hg at admission, atrial fibrillation, or cerebrovascular stenosis (≥70%) or were receiving intravenous thrombolytic therapy. Therefore, our findings may not apply to these populations. However, the proportion of patients with BP ≥220/120 mm Hg or treated with intravenous thrombolytic therapy is low in China, 12 , 32 and the baseline characteristics of the participants in this study were similar to those in the China National Stroke Registry. 33 Second, this was an observational study, so we were unable to establish a causal relationship between plasma polyamines and adverse clinical outcomes of ischemic stroke, despite adjusting for many important potential confounders. Third, we only measured plasma polyamine concentrations at baseline and were unable to investigate the relationships between the dynamic changes in these plasma polyamines and ischemic stroke outcomes. Fourth, the plasma samples were stored at −80 °C for ≈9 years until analysis by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. However, strict aliquoting and storage conditions minimized the impact on study results. Moreover, the detection of the 3 polyamines was conducted under consistent conditions, ensuring that their concentration trends remained unchanged over time. Furthermore, as far as we know, no similar studies have been conducted in patients with stroke using fresh plasma, making it challenging to establish comparisons. Further studies are needed to investigate this. Fifth, patients with cancer were excluded from the trial, and we did not assess other brain disorders such as Alzheimer disease; hence, we were unable to assess the influence of cancer status and other brain diseases on polyamine levels. Further studies are needed to validate our results.
sections.conclusion: Elevated plasma putrescine levels were associated with decreased risks of adverse outcomes after ischemic stroke, whereas elevated spermine levels were associated with increased risks of adverse outcomes. Further studies are warranted to explore deeply whether targeting these metabolites could be a meaningful strategy for the treatment of ischemic stroke.
